description: We are a unified, highly specialized team of AI Engineers, Computer Scientists, and Data Specialists. With a shared, deep-rooted background in Machine Learning, Deep Learning, and Computer Vision, we live and breathe data. We united to bring advanced technical expertise to the fields of Education and Data Visualization for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
FIRE-X is an interactive research platform that helps users explore and compare published space combustion experiments. Developed for the Flame in Freefall challenge, it connects NASA experimental tables and reports from studies such as BASS-II, FLEX, and Saffire in one searchable interface.
Users select a material, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and gravity context to find relevant experimental records. The platform displays available measurements, links findings to their sources, highlights missing data, and supports scenario saving and report export. It also includes a research document library and an interactive 3D reference enclosure.
FIRE-X addresses the difficulty of comparing experiments conducted under different conditions. It helps researchers, students, and spacecraft safety teams investigate published evidence and identify questions for further testing. The current prototype uses transparent matching rules. Its color indicator is explicitly illustrative, while flame spread values remain linked to specific published experiments. Future development will focus on laboratory validation and calibrated predictive models.
details:
FIRE-X is an interactive platform developed by Team Sadeem for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It helps users explore published microgravity combustion research, compare experimental conditions, and trace findings to their original sources.

Users begin by selecting a material, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, and gravity context. The platform applies transparent matching rules to retrieve relevant experimental records and highlight differences or missing information. Users can inspect source fields, compare records, search research documents, save scenarios, and export evidence reports.

Our prototype organizes 1,325 catalog records and 276 research documents. These include experimental tables, sample conditions, and extracted publication texts; the counts do not represent 1,325 independently verified experiments. NASA studies represented include BASS-II, FLEX, Saffire, SAME, SPICE, and ACME Flame Design. NIST ground-based PMMA measurements are presented separately to preserve the distinction between terrestrial and microgravity experiments.

The interface combines searchable evidence, charts, and an interactive 3D reference enclosure. Where available, it presents published gas measurements and flame-spread references with their experimental context. Missing measurements remain explicitly unavailable.

The current prototype does not contain a trained fire-risk prediction model. Its green, yellow, and red visualization uses an illustrative oxygen-based display index with arbitrary thresholds, not a validated probability of fire. Published flame-spread values are references from specific experiments, not predictions for the selected scenario. The 3D enclosure is a visualization, not a computational fluid dynamics simulation.

We built the application using Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, and SQLite. Document search uses SQLite FTS5 and BM25 ranking. The frontend uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js, and Three.js with STL loading. The demonstrated version operates through local evidence retrieval; optional language-model integration is available but was not activated.

Our contribution is bringing scenario comparison, source traceability, missing-data visibility, and accessible visualization into one workflow. We incorporated existing datasets and a reference enclosure from external resources, with attribution, while implementing the connected application and evidence-handling workflow.

The intended users are students, combustion researchers, and spacecraft safety research teams. We aim to make relevant evidence easier to discover and help users formulate questions for further experiments. Future work includes additional primary-source verification, expert evaluation, and predictive modeling only where suitable experimental labels and independent validation are available.

OpenAI Codex assisted with code generation, debugging, data-processing scripts, testing, documentation, translation, and presentation preparation.
